prompt: What is the defence against SQL injection that both box office services use in every query?
hint: Look for the ? in the SQL.

choices.text: Removing quotes from what the user typed
choices.why: It mangles names like O'Brien and misses other special characters.

choices.text: A firewall in front of the database server
choices.why: A firewall filters connections, not what a query means.

choices.text: Parameterised queries, with ? placeholders
choices.why: Right. The values travel apart from the SQL, so the database never reads them as SQL.

choices.text: Running the database as a user without privileges
choices.why: Least privilege limits the damage; it does not stop the query from being rewritten.

prompt: GET /search?q=' answered 200 with A Doll's House. What does that tell the tester?
hint: To the database, what was the quote?

choices.text: The quote was data: it matched a title as a letter
choices.why: Right. A query built by pasting would have failed on it with a 500.

choices.text: The search is vulnerable, as it returned a result
choices.why: It returned the one title containing an apostrophe, which is what a search should do.

choices.text: Nothing, because a quote is not a useful probe
choices.why: A quote is the character that breaks a pasted query; an ordinary answer is evidence.

choices.text: The service escaped the quote before the query ran
choices.why: Nothing escapes it: the value is a parameter and never part of the SQL.

prompt: The search for % returned all 20 shows although the query is parameterised. How should a tester record it?
hint: What can anybody already see at /shows?

choices.text: As a critical SQL injection that has to be fixed before the release ships
choices.why: The value never became SQL; LIKE read its own wildcard, and nothing private was reached.

choices.text: As a false positive that should simply be deleted from the report
choices.why: The behaviour is real; it is only harmless on this route.

choices.text: As a performance defect, since it returns far more rows than were asked for
choices.why: Twenty rows is the whole list on sale; the question is what it exposes.

choices.text: A note: wildcards in a value, harmless here, a finding on private data
choices.why: Right. Same behaviour, different verdict by context; the fix where it matters is ESCAPE.

prompt: In SQLite, a parameterised query marks where each value goes with the character ___.
hint: It appears in every query of app.py.

prompt: Which answer to the marker nft-probe shows that the page encoded it?
hint: What does a browser show for <?

choices.text: nft-probe, exactly as it was sent
choices.why: That is the markup sent as markup: the encoding is missing.

choices.text: <em>nft-probe</em>
choices.why: Right. The browser shows the angle brackets as text.

choices.text: nft-probe, with the tags removed
choices.why: Stripping is not encoding, and mangles real text elsewhere.

choices.text: A 400, because angle brackets are refused
choices.why: Refusing them on input breaks legitimate text; the defence is at the output.

prompt: Why does the lesson test the search term inside value="…" separately from the holder's name in the list?

choices.text: Attributes are never shown to the person using the page
choices.why: The value of a search box is shown, and the context still matters.

choices.text: Search terms are stored by the service, and names are not
choices.why: It is the other way round, and storage is not what decides the encoding.

choices.text: Inside value="…" the double quote ends the attribute
choices.why: Right. An escape that handled only < and > would pass the first check and fail this one.

choices.text: The CSP header covers the list but leaves the form uncovered
choices.why: CSP covers the whole page; the difference is the encoding context.

prompt: Match each layer to what it does on account.py's page.
hint: Three layers in the section, plus lesson 17.

pairs.right: lets the browser run no script on the page
keeps the session cookie out of reach of scripts
stops the browser guessing another type

right_distractors: checks the password against its hash

prompt: A developer proposes stripping < and > from every booking name when it is saved, instead of encoding on output. What does the lesson say is wrong with it?
hint: The same text lands in more than one context.

choices.text: It mangles real text and misses quotes, URLs and scripts
choices.why: Right. Each context needs its own encoding, which only the output knows.

choices.text: Nothing, since filtering the input is the standard defence
choices.why: Encoding belongs at the output, for the context the text lands in.

choices.text: It is slower than encoding
choices.why: Speed is not the objection; correctness is.

choices.text: Python cannot remove characters from a string it has stored
choices.why: It can; the problem is what that leaves undefended.

prompt: Why can another site not fill in account.py's CSRF token?

choices.text: The token is sent in a cookie it cannot set
choices.why: The token is in the form, not in a cookie.

choices.text: Browsers block every form posted between sites
choices.why: They do not; that is why CSRF exists.

choices.text: The token changes every second
choices.why: It lives as long as the session.

choices.text: It cannot read the page that holds the token, so it cannot copy it
choices.why: Right. It can make the browser send a form, but not see the value the service wrote into its own.

prompt: The form without its token got 403. Why does the lesson also send the same form with the token?
hint: A refusal on its own proves less than it seems.

choices.text: To check that the token has not expired in the meantime
choices.why: The token lives with the session; the point is the control.

choices.text: A route refusing every form would also pass the first check
choices.why: Right. The 303 proves the refusal is the token check and not a broken route.

choices.text: Because a 403 only counts as valid once a 303 has been seen too
choices.why: Status codes do not depend on each other like that.

choices.text: To clean up the booking the first request left
choices.why: Cancelling is the effect, not the reason for the request.

prompt: Why do account.py's JSON routes need no CSRF token while the cancel form does?
hint: Which credential does a browser attach on its own?

choices.text: JSON cannot be sent to a service from a page on another site
choices.why: Other sites can send JSON with scripts; what they lack is the header.

choices.text: The JSON routes are read-only and leave the bookings as they were
choices.why: POST /bookings creates a booking; it changes state.

choices.text: The Authorization header, which a browser does not add by itself to a request
choices.why: Right. Move them to cookie sessions and they would need a token too.

choices.text: SameSite protects JSON requests but not the HTML forms
choices.why: SameSite is about cookies, whatever the body type.

prompt: A CSV named notes.png was refused with 415. What did account.py look at?

choices.text: The first bytes of the content
choices.why: Right. A PNG or JPEG signature, or a refusal.

choices.text: The extension at the end of the file name
choices.why: The name said .png and was refused anyway.

choices.text: The Content-Type header the client sent
choices.why: A header is the client's claim, like the name.

choices.text: The size, which was too small for an image
choices.why: Size is checked against a maximum; the type comes from the bytes.

prompt: Put account.py's upload checks in the order the code makes them.
hint: Nothing is read before the size is known.
items: check the PNG or JPEG signature
write it under a random name

prompt: Why does account.py store an upload under 32 random hexadecimal digits instead of the name the client sent?

choices.text: Random names compress better
choices.why: Compression has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: To hide which customer uploaded it from the staff
choices.why: The owner is a separate question; the name is about paths.

choices.text: Because SQLite cannot store file names
choices.why: The file goes to the filesystem, not to SQLite.

choices.text: So nothing the client sent becomes part of a path
choices.why: Right. A client's name could carry slashes or dots that walk out of the directory.

prompt: With the line ending # CSRF check commented out, two of twelve tests fail. Which pair?

choices.text: The form that carries its token, and the escaped marker
choices.why: A form with its token still works; escaping is not touched by that line.

choices.text: A form without a token, and one from another session
choices.why: Right. One line guards both cases, and each case has a test naming it.

choices.text: The upload size and the upload type
choices.why: The uploads have their own checks on other lines.

choices.text: The quote in the search and the quote in a booking
choices.why: Those are held by parameterised queries, not by the CSRF check.

prompt: A new route lets customers rename a booking's holder and shows the new name on the page. Which pair of probes from this lesson does it need before release?
hint: It writes to the database and to the page.

choices.text: A file that is not an image, and one over 200 KB
choices.why: There is no upload on that route.

choices.text: A form without a token, and a percent sign
choices.why: A form test is right if it is a form; the percent sign only matters for LIKE searches.

choices.text: Quote kept, marker escaped
choices.why: Right. One for the database, one for the page; if it is a cookie form, the token test too.

choices.text: Five wrong passwords, and an expired session
choices.why: Those test sign-in, which the route does not change.
